final_proof:
Write I for the identity functor on C, and write 1_X for the identity morphism of an object X of C. Let X = (E, *, g) be an object of (I ↓ F). By the definition of a comma category, E is an object of C and g: I(E) → F(*). Since I(E) = E and F(*) = C, this says precisely that g: E → C. Hence g is an object of the slice category C/C, so the object assignment J(E, *, g) = g is well-defined.

Now let (k, id_*): (E, *, g) → (E′, *, g′) be a morphism in the comma category. Thus k: E → E′ is a morphism of C, and the comma-category compatibility condition is

F(id_*) ∘ g = g′ ∘ I(k).

Because F(id_*) = 1_C and I(k) = k, this condition reduces to

g = g′ ∘ k.

But this is exactly the condition that k be a morphism from the slice object g: E → C to the slice object g′: E′ → C. Therefore the morphism assignment J(k, id_*) = k is well-defined and has the required source and target.

It remains to verify the functor axioms. The identity morphism of (E, *, g) in the comma category is (1_E, id_*). Consequently,

J(1_E, id_*) = 1_E,

and 1_E is precisely the identity morphism of the slice object g: E → C. Thus J preserves identities.

Finally, suppose (k, id_*): (E, *, g) → (E′, *, g′) and (ℓ, id_*): (E′, *, g′) → (E″, *, g″) are composable morphisms in the comma category. Composition there is componentwise, so

(ℓ, id_*) ∘ (k, id_*) = (ℓ ∘ k, id_*).

It follows that

J((ℓ, id_*) ∘ (k, id_*)) = ℓ ∘ k = J(ℓ, id_*) ∘ J(k, id_*),

where the composition on the right is composition in the slice category, inherited from C. Hence J preserves composition. Therefore J: (I ↓ F) → C/C is a covariant functor.
